nodes.title: The conjecture: Landau ⇒ binary x-ray
nodes.intuition: Put n stones on a plank with marks −(n−1) … n−1, at most one per mark; the start has a stone on every other mark. A stone's score is the number of empty marks to its left. Landau's condition says that, for every k, the k leftmost stones have at least as many empty marks to their left in total as at the start, with equality for all n stones: no group of left stones has drifted left, and the whole is balanced. A witness is a board with one point in each row and column whose points sit on exactly the stones' diagonals. The four-views tab shows the same question as stones, grid, matching and Skolem arcs. Claim: every arrangement satisfying Landau's condition has a witness.

pics.cap: Start: 4 stones on every other mark
The arrangement {−2, −1, +1, +2} and a witness, 2 4 1 3

nodes.statement: Let D = {d₁<…<dₙ} be n distinct diagonals (d = column − row) of the n×n board, and s_k = d_k + n − k. If s satisfies Landau (Σ_{i≤k} s_i ≥ C(k,2) for all k, with equality at k = n), then some permutation uses each diagonal of D exactly once (a witness). Necessity is proved: the points on the k lowest diagonals sit in k different rows and columns, so their diagonals sum to at least (k leftmost columns) − (k bottom rows). BMPS 2005 Conj. 5 = Nordh 2008 Conj. 10.
nodes.evidence: Exhaustively verified for n ≤ 22 (Devin round 1). Open as of 2026.
nodes.refs: Bebeacua–Mansour–Postnikov–Severini 2005; Nordh, Perfect Skolem sets, Discrete Math 308 (2008); Brualdi–Fritscher, Hankel and Toeplitz X-rays of permutations, LAA 449 (2014) (not yet read)

nodes.title: The conjecture for arrangements with no tight cut
nodes.intuition: A tight cut is a place on the plank where the stones to its left have exactly as many empty marks to their left as at the start: that group hasn't drifted right at all. Arrangements with no such place are the core case. Claim: every valid arrangement with no tight cut has a witness.
nodes.statement: Every valid D whose Landau inequalities are strict for every k < n has a witness.

nodes.title: Tight cuts split
nodes.intuition: If the left k stones haven't drifted at all, their points are squeezed into the bottom-left k×k corner of the board, and the other points into the top-right corner. Each corner is a smaller board of the same kind. Claim: a tight cut splits the arrangement into two smaller valid ones, and solutions of those two drop into the corners to solve the whole.

pics.cap: {−4,−3,−2,+2,+3,+4}: tight cut after three stones; two 3×3 corners

nodes.statement: If Σ_{i≤k} s_i = C(k,2) for some k < n, then D_low = {d₁…d_k} + (n−k) and D_high = {d_{k+1}…d_n} − k are valid at sizes k and n − k, and if both have witnesses, so does D (their skew sum).
nodes.proof: Equality at k says the k lowest diagonals add up to −k(n−k), the smallest total possible for k points in different rows and columns; that minimum forces those k points into the bottom k rows and the leftmost k columns. So D splits into the lower k stones (shifted up by n−k) and the upper n−k stones (shifted down by k). Both shifted sets inherit Landau's inequalities from the prefix sums, with equality at their own sizes, so they are valid smaller instances. Put a witness of the first in the bottom-left k×k block and a witness of the second in the top-right block: the shifts put every point back on its original diagonal.

nodes.title: Block layouts glue solutions
nodes.intuition: Cut the board into a grid of blocks. A small permutation σ picks one block in each block-row and block-column, and each picked block holds a smaller solved board. Every point in a block is shifted by the same amount, the block's offset: the column it starts in minus the row it starts in. On the plank, a block is a group of stones that is a shifted copy of a smaller arrangement, centred at the block's offset. In the picture, σ = 2413 holds blocks of sizes 1, 1, 3, 1, and the 3×3 block carries the solution 321 of {−2, 0, +2}, shifted by −2. Claim: if the stones split into groups, each group (recentred) has a solution, and the group sizes and centres fit some block layout, then the whole arrangement has a solution.

pics.cap: π = 4 6 3 2 1 5: σ = 2413 with blocks of sizes 1, 1, 3, 1
Groups: {−4, −2, 0} around −2 (the 3×3 block), and {−1}, {+3}, {+4} alone

nodes.statement: Let D split into groups G₁…G_k of sizes n_i with integer means c_i. If each G_i − c_i has a witness, and there are an order of the groups by rows and an order by columns (a permutation σ) with c_i = (total size of the groups before i in the column order) − (total size of the groups before i in the row order), then D has a witness (the inflation σ[π₁,…,π_k]).
nodes.proof: Let π_i be a witness of G_i − c_i (size n_i). Give block i the rows after the groups that precede it in the row order, and the columns after the groups that precede it in the column order; by hypothesis, column start − row start = c_i. A point of π_i at local position (r, c) lands at (row start + r, column start + c), so its diagonal is its local diagonal plus c_i, which lies in G_i. Blocks use disjoint rows and disjoint columns, so the result is a permutation, and since the groups partition D, every diagonal of D is used exactly once.

nodes.title: Direct sums glue (Nordh Thm 27)
nodes.intuition: Two solved boards placed corner to corner along the main diagonal make a bigger board whose points keep their diagonals. Unlike a tight cut, the two sets of stones can interleave on the plank, so the result can have no tight cut. Claim: two solved boards with disjoint diagonal sets combine this way into a solution of the union.
nodes.statement: If π₁ witnesses D₁ (size n₁), π₂ witnesses D₂ (size n₂), and D₁ ∩ D₂ = ∅, then π₁ ⊕ π₂ witnesses D₁ ∪ D₂.
nodes.proof: Place π₁ in the top-left n₁×n₁ block and π₂ in the bottom-right block. Each point keeps its diagonal (both blocks sit on the main diagonal), rows and columns are disjoint between the blocks, and the diagonals don't collide because D₁ ∩ D₂ = ∅.

nodes.title: Fixed-point reduction
nodes.intuition: A stone on the middle mark can go in the top-left corner: that uses row 1 and column 1 and changes no other cell's diagonal. Claim: if the other stones form a solvable arrangement one size smaller, the whole arrangement is solvable with that corner point.

pics.cap: Corner point on diagonal 0; the 4×4 board below uses {±1, ±2}

nodes.statement: If 0 ∈ D and D ∖ {0} has a witness at size n − 1, then D has a witness with π(1) = 1.
nodes.proof: Put a point at (1,1); it is on diagonal 0 and uses row 1 and column 1. Deleting them leaves rows and columns 2…n, and every remaining cell keeps its diagonal. So a witness of D∖{0} at size n−1, shifted down and right by one, fills the rest.

nodes.title: Every arrangement but P_n splits into blocks
nodes.intuition: To split an arrangement, partition its stones into groups that each balance around a whole-number centre, such that each group moved back to the middle is a valid smaller arrangement, and the group sizes and centres can be laid out as blocks. In the example, {−3, −2, −1, 0, +2, +4} splits as {−3, −1} around −2, {−2, 0} around −1, and {+2}, {+4} alone; the layout 2413 with block sizes 1, 1, 2, 2 puts every block at its centre. Both choices — the grouping and the layout — are searches, and the layout is itself a placement puzzle with wide blocks of the same total size. So this claim is not a reduction to smaller cases: the blocks are smaller, but the layout is not, and the claim is at least as strong as the conjecture. Claim: every valid arrangement with no tight cut except P_n splits this way.

pics.cap: The layout: pattern 2413, block sizes 1, 1, 2, 2

nodes.statement: For n ≥ 4, every valid no-tight-cut D other than P_n splits into k < n groups satisfying the hypotheses of the block-layout lemma: integer means c_i, each G_i − c_i valid at its size, and the layout of sizes and centres realizable by some σ.
nodes.evidence: Exhaustive for 4 ≤ n ≤ 12: exactly one no-tight-cut D per n fails, P_n (up to mirror, out of 1, 3, 5, 15, 36, 107, 306, 969, 3055). Checked through witnesses (D splits iff some witness is not a simple permutation), so it relies on the conjecture at those sizes, which is verified. The layout can need up to n − 1 blocks.

nodes.title: The prime arrangement P_n is solvable
nodes.intuition: P_n is the no-tight-cut arrangement closest to the start: stones on every other mark, except that each end pair is squeezed together. It is the one arrangement that can't be split into blocks, so it needs its own solution. The solution is two interleaved staircases plus two corner points. Claim: the formula gives a solution for every n.

pics.cap: P₆
The formula at n = 6: 4 6 2 5 1 3

nodes.statement: P_n (scores 1, 1, 2, 3, …, n−3, n−2, n−2; D = {±(n−2)} ∪ {|d| ≤ n−3, d ≡ n−1 mod 2}) has a witness for every n ≥ 4: π(2) = n; π(i) = n−1−i for odd i ≤ n−2; π(i) = n+3−i for even i ≥ 4; and π(n−1) = 1 (n even) or π(n) = 2 (n odd).
nodes.refs: Verify agent 2026-11-23, /home/claude/agents/verify/pn.py (formula checked n ≤ 30; exactly two witnesses for n ≤ 14)
nodes.proof: Odd positions i ≤ n−2 get the values n−1−i and even positions i ≥ 4 get n+3−i: two staircases using opposite parity classes of values, so together with n (at position 2) and the leftover value they form a permutation. Diagonals: n−2 at i = 2, 2−n at the leftover position, n−1−2i at odd i and n−1−2(i−2) at even i ≥ 4. The last two together give every n−1−2r for 1 ≤ r ≤ n−2, i.e. {n−3, n−5, …, 3−n}, which is the rest of P_n.

nodes.title: Every arrangement but P_n has a 2×2 block
nodes.intuition: A 2×2 block is two points in neighbouring rows and neighbouring columns, the upper one a step to the right. On the plank it is two stones two marks apart; in a block layout it becomes one fat stone at their midpoint, with every other stone alone. Example: in 2 6 5 4 1 3 (stones −4, −3, 0, +1, +2, +4), rows 3–4 and columns 4–5 hold a block on diagonals 0 and +2. Shrinking the block to one point usually leaves a permutation that repeats a diagonal, so this does not reduce to a smaller instance of the same problem. Laying out one fat stone and n − 2 thin ones is still a full-size placement puzzle, so this claim is stronger than the conjecture: it says every arrangement has a solution of a special shape. Its value is that it narrows what kind of solution to look for. Claim: every valid arrangement with no tight cut except P_n has a solution with a 2×2 block.

pics.cap: Rows 3–4, columns 4–5: a 2×2 block on diagonals 0 and +2

nodes.statement: Every valid no-tight-cut D other than P_n has stones x, x + 2 such that some witness contains a 2×2 block (points (r, c+1) and (r+1, c)) on those two diagonals. Equivalently, the layout with one 2-wide stone at offset x + 1 and all other stones 1-wide is solvable.
nodes.evidence: Exhaustive for no-tight-cut D up to mirror, n = 4–14 (33,284 D at n = 14); the only exception at each n is P_n. Also exact there: shrinking a 2×2 block never leaves an arrangement with a tight cut. A block (any size) whose shrunken permutation has distinct diagonals does not always exist: 1, 2, 3, 5, 11 arrangements at n = 5–9 have none (first beyond P_n: ±{1, 2, 3}).

nodes.title: Rule: the pair nearest the middle
nodes.intuition: A natural way to pick the block: among stones two marks apart, take the pair centred nearest the middle. Claim: that pair always works.

pics.cap: It picks {−1, +1}, but only {−3, −1} and {+1, +3} form blocks

nodes.statement: For every valid no-tight-cut D ≠ P_n, the pair {x, x + 2} ⊂ D whose centre x + 1 is closest to 0 forms a 2×2 block in some witness.
nodes.evidence: First failure n = 6, D = ±{1, 2, 3} (picture). Right for 99.3% of D up to n = 14, but failures grow (424 at n = 14). Also failed: the leftmost pair, any pair with an empty mark between, pairs whose outer neighbours are empty.

nodes.title: Rule: merge the pair into one stone
nodes.intuition: The simplest reduction: replace two stones two marks apart by one stone between them and solve the smaller arrangement. Claim: some pair can always be merged into a valid smaller arrangement.

pics.cap: No pair is centred at 0, so every merge leaves the stones unbalanced

nodes.statement: For every valid no-tight-cut D ≠ P_n, some pair {x, x + 2} ⊂ D has D ∖ {x, x+2} ∪ {x+1} valid at size n − 1.
nodes.evidence: A valid arrangement's stones sum to 0, but the merged set sums to −(x + 1), so only a pair centred at 0 can work. D = {−4, −3, 0, 1, 2, 4} has no such pair (picture); overall only 7.7% of pairs pass.

nodes.title: An exact test for fat-stone layouts
nodes.intuition: Replace a pair of stones by one 2-wide fat stone at their midpoint. A Landau-style count over all groups of stones is clearly necessary for such a layout to be solvable. Claim: the count is also sufficient.

pics.cap: Fat stone at −1 from {−2, 0}: passes the count, but no solution has that block

nodes.statement: A layout of stones of width 1 or 2 with target offsets t (total width W; row and column orders free) is solvable iff for every set S of stones with total width V, Σ_S width·t ≥ −V(W − V).
nodes.evidence: False: D = {−4, −2, 0, 1, 2, 3} with {−2, 0} fattened passes the count, yet no witness has that block (the pairs {−4, −2}, {0, 2}, {+1, +3} do). Failures are common (117 of 260 in one class at total width 8), and parity gives no fix.

nodes.title: Bounded frames build everything
nodes.intuition: Every permutation is a frame with blocks filled in: shrink each maximal block to a point and what remains is the frame, a permutation with no blocks of its own (or 12 / 21 when the board splits corner to corner). Repeating this inside the blocks gives a tree of frames. Example: 3 6 2 1 5 4 is the frame 2413 with two of its points widened into 21. A frame may itself repeat a diagonal — the widening shifts the stones around it and can fix that. The claim: a fixed finite list of small frames, together with P_k's own solutions, is enough to build a solution of every arrangement. Then all the difficulty would sit in a finite list plus one explicit family.

pics.cap: Frame 2413 (P₄'s solution) with two points widened into 21

nodes.statement: There is a constant K such that every valid D has a witness whose substitution tree uses only the frames 12, 21, the solutions of the P_k, and block-free permutations with at most K points.
nodes.evidence: For n ≤ 9 a greedy search found 23 frames of size ≤ 8 that, together with 12, 21 and P_k's solutions, build a witness of every valid D (mirrors and tight cuts included; checked recursively at every level). The frames needed per size so far: 1, 3, 8, 6, 4 for sizes 4–8; about half repeat a diagonal (e.g. 3 1 5 2 4, which builds ±{1, 2, 3}). Whether the sizes stay bounded as n grows is unknown. Interactive builder and data: Block-building experiments page.

nodes.title: Rule: only P_k's solutions as frames
nodes.intuition: The P_k are the only arrangements that can't be split, so their solutions are the natural building blocks. Claim: gluing and P_k's solutions are all the frames ever needed.

pics.cap: ±{1, 2, 3}: each of its 6 solutions needs another frame

nodes.statement: Every valid D has a witness whose substitution tree uses only the frames 12, 21 and the solutions of the P_k.
nodes.evidence: False at n = 6 for ±{1, 2, 3}: two of its solutions are block-free themselves, and the others have frames like 3 1 5 2 4 or 2 5 1 6 4 3. Misses 1, 3, 17, 79 arrangements at n = 6–9.

nodes.title: Rule: symmetric block-free frames
nodes.intuition: Instead of a fixed list of frames, allow a whole describable family: every block-free frame that folds onto itself across the main diagonal or looks the same after a half turn. P_k's solutions are of this kind. Claim: these frames build a solution of every arrangement.

pics.cap: A half-turn-symmetric block-free solution, usable as a frame

nodes.statement: Every valid D has a witness whose substitution tree uses only 12, 21 and block-free permutations that are involutions or centrosymmetric (survive a half turn).
nodes.evidence: With only frames that are themselves solutions (no repeated diagonal): builds everything for n ≤ 7, misses 4 arrangements at n = 8 and 26 at n = 9 (no tight cut, mirrors counted). Allowing symmetric frames that repeat a diagonal (e.g. 4 6 3 1 5 2): misses 2 at n = 8 (the Q₈ pair) and 18 at n = 9. The remaining misses need asymmetric frames such as 5 2 6 4 1 3, 3 1 5 2 4, 5 7 4 2 6 1 3; adding frames greedily, 12 more (10 of them repeating a diagonal) fix everything to n = 9.
nodes.refs: Basket agent 2026-11-23, symfam.py, symall.py, symfix.py; Block-building experiments page

nodes.title: One move past P_n: two P pieces and a slide
nodes.intuition: Start from two solved pieces stacked corner to corner: one in the top rows, one in the bottom rows, the bottom one entirely to the left. That is a skew sum and always has a tight cut. Now slide the bottom piece's rightmost column two places to the right. Only three stones move: the bottom piece's point goes up two diagonals, and the two top points it passes each go down one. That is exactly one inward move on the stones, across the cut. Example: 3142 over 2413 with the slide gives 7 4 8 5 2 6 1 3, a solution of Q₈. Claim: every arrangement one move past P_n is built this way from two P pieces, with the cut where the move is.

pics.cap: 3142 over 2413: skew sum (tight cut), then the slide gives Q₈

nodes.statement: Let D be valid with no tight cut and one minimal move past P_n (so D has n − 1 three-cycles; Q_n, the central move, is one of them). Then D has a witness of this form: a solution of P_a (or 21, 132/213 for a = 2, 3) in the top a rows, a solution of P_b in the bottom b = n − a rows, columns as in a skew sum except that the bottom piece's rightmost column slides two places right, past the top piece's two leftmost columns.
nodes.evidence: Holds for every such D at n = 8, 9, 10 (2, 3, 3 arrangements up to mirror), and for Q_n for n = 7–12 (exactly one such splice each). All have exactly 4 witnesses (P_n has 2).

nodes.title: Two moves past P_n: a chain of three P pieces
nodes.intuition: The next layer out from P_n. If one move past P_n is two P pieces and one slide, two moves might be three P pieces and two slides. Claim: that always works.

pics.cap: 21, 213, 213 stacked, with slides at both cuts

nodes.statement: Every valid no-tight-cut D two minimal moves past P_n has a witness that is a chain of P pieces (solutions of P_k, or 1, 21, 132, 213), skew-stacked, with one slide of length at most 4 (either direction) at each cut.
nodes.evidence: Works for every such D at n = 8 and 10 and all but one at n = 9 (all have exactly 8 witnesses). Fails for D = {−7, −5, −4, −3, 0, 3, 4, 5, 7} at n = 9 (chains of up to 6 pieces, slides up to 4); its witnesses use pieces like 321 instead (e.g. 8 7 6 4 9 3 2 1 5).

nodes.title: A minimal move adds exactly one 3-cycle
nodes.intuition: A minimal move takes two stones whose scores are s and s + 2 and makes them both s + 1 (everything between them is full, so nothing else changes rank). That lowers the sum of squared scores by exactly 2, which is one more 3-cycle. So 'k moves past P_n' is a property of the arrangement, not of the route: it means k more 3-cycles than P_n.

pics.cap: P_6 (scores 1 1 2 3 4 4, 4 three-cycles) → Q_6 (scores 1 1 3 3 3 4, 5 three-cycles)

nodes.statement: If E is obtained from D by one minimal move, then t(E) = t(D) + 1, where t(D) = C(n,3) − Σ C(s_i, 2) is the number of 3-cycles of any tournament with D's scores. So every sequence of minimal moves from D to E has length t(E) − t(D).
nodes.evidence: Direct computation.

nodes.title: Short-slide grammar builds a witness for every arrangement
nodes.intuition: This is the pattern from the layers past P_n made into a rule: pieces stacked with short slides, and points widened into blocks. It is a strengthening of the conjecture, not a reduction. The slide limit matters: with unlimited slides the rule covers everything for a trivial reason, because a one-row top piece with any slide just means 'add a new top row anywhere', which is peeling the top row.

pics.cap: Counterexample {±1, ±2, ±3}: a solution, 2 4 6 1 3 5, two interleaved staircases; none of its 6 solutions is in G

nodes.statement: Let G be the smallest set of permutations with distinct diagonals that contains every P_k solution, 1, 21, 132, 213 and every anti-diagonal, and is closed under (a) skew-stacking two members with one column slid across the cut by at most 2, and (b) widening each point of a member into a member. Claim: every valid no-tight-cut D has a witness in G.
nodes.evidence: Covers every D at n ≤ 9 up to 12 moves past P_n, including the n = 9 exception to the three-piece chain. Fails for {±1, ±2, ±3} at n = 6 (4 moves past P_6, the most central arrangement), 1 at n = 7, 2 at n = 8, 6 at n = 9, all 13 or more moves past P_n at n = 9.

nodes.title: Symmetric arrangements are solvable
nodes.intuition: Symmetric means the plank looks the same in a mirror held at the middle mark: every stone at +d has a partner at −d, so the x-ray reads the same forwards and backwards. Claim: every symmetric arrangement with no tight cut has a solution.

pics.cap: Symmetric: 0, ±2, ±3, ±5
One of its solutions, 3 7 6 1 5 4 2

nodes.statement: Let 𝒩 be the valid arrangements with no tight cut and 𝒮 ⊂ 𝒩 the symmetric ones (D = −D). Every D ∈ 𝒮 has a witness.

nodes.title: Non-symmetric arrangements are solvable
nodes.intuition: A non-symmetric arrangement has a different mirror image. Flipping a solution across the main diagonal turns it into a solution of the mirror image, so each mirror pair stands or falls together. Claim: every non-symmetric arrangement with no tight cut has a solution.

pics.cap: An arrangement and its mirror image
A solution of the first, 1 4 6 5 3 2

nodes.statement: Every D ∈ 𝒩 ∖ 𝒮 (no tight cut, D ≠ −D) has a witness.

nodes.title: Odd symmetric arrangements fold
nodes.intuition: With an odd number of symmetric stones, one sits on the middle mark. A solution that folds onto itself across the main diagonal puts that stone's point on the diagonal and pairs every other point with its mirror image. So a folding solution is a pairing puzzle: leave one position free and pair up the rest so that the pair distances are exactly the stones' distances from the middle. Claim: for every odd symmetric arrangement with no tight cut, the puzzle has a solution for a suitable free position.

pics.cap: {0, ±1, ±3}: positions paired (1,4) and (2,3), position 5 free

nodes.statement: If D ∈ 𝒮 has n = 2m + 1 and L = D ∩ (0, ∞), then for some position f the positions {1, …, n} ∖ {f} split into pairs with distances exactly L; equivalently, D has an involution witness with fixed point (f, f). (In terms of L, Landau says: the K largest elements of L sum to at most K(n − K), for every K.)
nodes.evidence: Holds for every symmetric valid D with n odd ≤ 15 (1971 at n = 15). No fixed choice of the free position works (end, centre and start all fail by n = 7), and 'parity + density for the remaining positions ⇒ pairing' is false (n = 5, L = {1, 3}, centre free). No theorem in the Skolem literature covers arbitrary L.

nodes.title: Even symmetric arrangements are solvable
nodes.intuition: With an even number of symmetric stones the middle mark is empty, and every stone at +d has a partner at −d. Claim: every such arrangement with no tight cut has a solution.

pics.cap: ±{1, 2, 5, 6}: eight stones, middle mark empty

nodes.statement: Every D ∈ 𝒮 with n even has a witness.

nodes.title: Even pairings exist (Nordh's Conjecture 8)
nodes.intuition: A solution that folds onto itself across the main diagonal pairs each point with its mirror image, so it is a pairing of positions 1…2m whose pair distances are exactly the stones' distances from the middle. A pair at an even distance joins two positions of the same parity; since there are equally many odd and even positions, the even distances must come in an even number. Example: L = {1, 2, 5, 6} has two even distances and pairs as (3,4), (5,7), (1,6), (2,8). Claim: for every even symmetric arrangement with no tight cut and an even number of even distances, such a pairing exists.
nodes.statement: Let D ∈ 𝒮 with n = 2m and L = D ∩ (0, ∞), and suppose L has an even number of even elements. Then positions 1…2m split into pairs with distances exactly L; equivalently, D has an involution witness. (The no-tight-cut case of Nordh's Conjecture 8: parity + density ⇒ perfect Skolem set.)
nodes.evidence: For even n ≤ 14, a symmetric valid D has an involution witness exactly when L has an even number of even elements. Nordh checked his conjecture for up to 20 distances. Proved special cases: Skolem ({1…m}), Langford/Simpson (intervals), Shalaby (an interval minus one element).

nodes.title: Half-turn solutions when folding is impossible
nodes.intuition: When L has an odd number of even distances, no solution can fold across the main diagonal. The next symmetry to try is a half turn of the board. A half-turn solution is determined by its top half, which gives a half-size puzzle: pick a permutation σ of 1…m, and for each row i use either the distance |σ(i) − i| (the point and its twin stay on their own sides) or the crossing distance 2m + 1 − i − σ(i) (they cross to the mirrored half); the chosen distances must be exactly L. Claim: every even symmetric arrangement with no tight cut and an odd number of even distances has a half-turn-symmetric solution.

pics.cap: L = {2, 3, 4, 6} (three even distances): no solution folds, but 4 8 7 6 3 2 1 5 survives a half turn

nodes.statement: Let D ∈ 𝒮 with n = 2m and L = D ∩ (0, ∞), and suppose L has an odd number of even elements. Then D has a centrosymmetric witness: π(n+1−i) = n+1−π(i).
nodes.evidence: Holds for every such D with n even ≤ 14. Narrower versions fail at n = 6 for L = {1, 2, 3}: σ an involution, or a pairing plus one 4-cycle.

nodes.title: F1: everything but the middle
nodes.intuition: Stones on every mark within distance a of the middle, with the middle mark empty. From above the solution is two parallel lines of slope 2, the top half on even columns and the bottom half on odd ones. Claim: this gives a solution for every a.
nodes.statement: For every a ≥ 1, D = {±1, …, ±a} (n = 2a) has the witness π(i) = 2i for i ≤ a, π(i) = 2i − (2a+1) for i > a.
nodes.refs: Nordh 2008, Thm 28 (arXiv v1 numbering); explicit witness ours
nodes.proof: Rows i ≤ a go to column 2i, so diagonal 2i − i = i takes the values 1…a on the even columns 2, 4, …, 2a. Rows i > a go to column 2i − 2a − 1, so diagonal i − 2a − 1 takes the values −a…−1 on the odd columns 1, 3, …, 2a − 1. All columns are distinct, so this is a permutation using each diagonal ±1…±a once.

nodes.title: The odd centre folds into a Skolem pairing
nodes.intuition: With an odd number of stones, the most central arrangement fills every mark from −m to m. A solution that folds across the main diagonal pairs up the positions with pair distances 1, 2, …, m and leaves one position as a fixed point. Pairing positions with distances 1…m is exactly a Skolem sequence, and when m ≡ 2, 3 mod 4 a 'hooked' one with a gap next to the end. Claim: these always give a solution.

pics.cap: m = 3 (hooked): pairs (1,2) (3,5) (4,7), position 6 fixed

nodes.statement: For n = 2m + 1, D = {−m, …, m} has an involution witness: from a Skolem sequence of order m (m ≡ 0, 1 mod 4; fixed point at position n) or a hooked Skolem sequence of order m (m ≡ 2, 3 mod 4; fixed point at position n − 1).
nodes.evidence: Skolem sequences exist iff m ≡ 0, 1 mod 4; hooked Skolem sequences iff m ≡ 2, 3 mod 4. Checked by search for n ≤ 11.

nodes.title: The most central arrangement is solvable
nodes.intuition: Moves only ever squeeze stones together, so they end at one most-crowded arrangement: every mark near the middle filled (the middle mark empty when n is even). In score terms the scores are as equal as possible, which is why it is unique. This is the opposite end from P_n, which has the fewest 3-cycles among arrangements without a tight cut. Both ends have explicit solutions. Claim: the centre is solvable for every n.

pics.cap: C₆ = ±{1, 2, 3}: two interleaved staircases (F1)
C₇ = {−3…3}: a folding solution (Skolem)

nodes.statement: For every n, the valid D with the most 3-cycles is unique, namely C_n = {−⌊n/2⌋, …, ⌊n/2⌋} with 0 removed when n is even, and C_n has a witness.
nodes.evidence: Uniqueness: the number of 3-cycles is C(n,3) − Σ C(s_i,2), maximised exactly when the scores differ by at most 1; checked n ≤ 12.

nodes.title: F3: folding solutions are Skolem pairings
nodes.intuition: A solution that folds onto itself across the main diagonal pairs each point (i, j) with its twin (j, i), on diagonals +(j − i) and −(j − i). So folding solutions of ±L are exactly ways to pair up positions with pair distances L, a classical Skolem/Langford puzzle; known solutions of that puzzle give infinite families of solved arrangements. Claim: folding solutions and such pairings correspond one to one.

pics.cap: Positions paired (1,5) (2,4) (3,6): distances 4, 2, 3

nodes.statement: D = ±L (n = 2m) has an involution witness ⇔ positions 1…2m split into pairs with distances exactly L; with one unpaired position, the same holds for D = {0} ∪ ±L. Known solvable L: {1…m} iff m ≡ 0, 1 mod 4 (Skolem 1957); intervals {d…d+m−1} under Simpson's 1983 conditions; {1…k} ∖ {j} on positions 1…2k−2 when k ≡ 0, 1 mod 4 and j odd, or k ≡ 2, 3 mod 4 and j even (Shalaby; Nordh Cor 26).
nodes.refs: Nordh 2008, Thm 23 and Cor 26; Skolem 1957; Simpson 1983; Shalaby
nodes.proof: An involution's 2-cycles i ↔ j give the points (i, j) and (j, i), on diagonals +(j − i) and −(j − i). So an involution witness for ±L is the same thing as a pairing of the positions with distances exactly L, and a fixed point adds diagonal 0. Skolem (1957) shows {1…2m} pairs with distances {1…m} iff m ≡ 0, 1 (mod 4); Simpson (1983) settles distances {d…d+m−1}, and Shalaby's near-Skolem theorem settles {1…k} ∖ {m} on positions 1…2k−2.

nodes.title: Minimal moves reach every arrangement
nodes.intuition: A minimal move slides two stones one mark toward each other when the marks just inside them are empty and everything between those is filled. The picture walks from the start to {−2, −1, +1, +2} in two moves. Claim: these moves, starting from 'every other mark', reach every valid arrangement.

pics.cap: Move 1: −3 and +1 slide in to −2 and 0
Move 2: 0 and +3 slide in to +1 and +2

nodes.statement: Call a move minimal if it takes stones at a < b, where a + 1 and b − 1 are empty and every mark strictly between them is occupied, to a + 1 and b − 1. Every valid D is reached from the start (stones on every other mark) by minimal moves, and each move raises the number of 3-cycles by exactly 1.
nodes.proof: Induct on the number of 3-cycles. A non-transitive valid D has two equal scores; take a maximal run of equal scores v and undo a move at its two ends (v, v → v−1, v+1). The result stays sorted, its prefix sums drop by 1 only inside the run, and none of those prefixes can be tight (a tight prefix at k forces s_k < s_{k+1}), so it is still valid with one fewer 3-cycle. Each forward move only raises prefix sums, so it keeps Landau.

nodes.title: Minimal moves keep the board solvable
nodes.intuition: This is the step of an induction whose invariant is simply 'has a solution': the start has exactly one solution, so if every minimal move kept a solution, every arrangement would have one. All of the difficulty sits in this step. Claim: whenever an arrangement has a solution, so does the result of any minimal move.

pics.cap: The start for n = 5 and a solution after one move

nodes.statement: If D has a witness and D → D′ is a minimal move, then D′ has a witness.

nodes.title: A move never loses more than a fixed fraction
nodes.intuition: Count the solutions before and after a move. If a move could never lose more than a fixed fraction of them, solvability would pass along every move. In every test the worst loss comes from the same local picture of seven marks. Claim: some fixed fraction c of the solutions always survives.

pics.cap: The worst move: solutions drop to exactly 2/3

nodes.statement: There is c > 0 with W(D′) ≥ c·W(D) for every minimal move D → D′ and every n.
nodes.evidence: Minimum ratio = 2/3 for n ≤ 16, attained only by this pattern; next-smallest ≈ 0.734 (n = 14–16).

nodes.title: Some solution needs only a small fix
nodes.intuition: After a move, some old solution can usually be fixed by swapping the columns of the two moving points: when the lower point sits the right number of rows below the upper one, the swap moves each onto the next diagonal inward and nothing else changes. When no solution is in that position, changing one or two more rows has always been enough. Claim: some old solution always becomes a new one after changing at most four rows.

pics.cap: Move −4, −1 → −3, −2: rows 3 and 5 swap columns 1 and 2

nodes.statement: For every minimal move D → D′ of a solvable D, some witness of D becomes a witness of D′ by changing at most 4 rows (the two moving stones' rows plus at most two more).
nodes.evidence: Best old solution, all minimal moves of all valid D, n ≤ 12: a plain column swap works for 93% of moves (41,726 of 44,972 at n = 12), including every move with nothing between the movers; the rest need 3 or 4 rows, never more. From an arbitrary old solution the fix grows (up to 7 rows at n = 12).

nodes.title: Bounded repair from any solution
nodes.intuition: Instead of choosing a good old solution, fix whichever one you have. Claim: the fix never needs more than a fixed number of other points to move.
nodes.statement: There is R such that for every minimal move D → D′ and every witness π of D, some witness of D′ agrees with π on all but at most R of the non-moving stones' points.
nodes.example:
n = 7: D = {−5,−2,−1,0,1,2,5}, move −5,−2 → −4,−3,
π = 3 7 1 4 6 5 2: every witness after the move
moves ≥ 3 of the other 5 points.
nodes.evidence: The worst case grows: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3 for n = 4–9, and 5 at n = 14 (Devin).

nodes.title: Fibrewise 2/3 bound
nodes.intuition: Freeze every point except the two moving ones, and compare how many ways the moving pair can be placed before and after. Claim: the count never drops below 2/3.
nodes.statement: For every minimal move and every placement of the non-moving stones' points that extends to a witness of D, it extends to at least 2/3 as many witnesses of D′.
nodes.evidence: Every fibre has size 0 or 1, so a fibre with one witness before and none after is a counterexample; these occur from small n.

nodes.title: All solutions connected by small rotations
nodes.intuition: If all solutions of an arrangement were linked by small steps, we could walk from any solution to one where a move is easy to fix. Claim: some fixed step size links them all.

pics.cap: P₄'s two solutions differ in every row: no small step links them

nodes.statement: There is k such that for every D, any two witnesses are connected by a chain of witnesses, each obtained from the previous by rearranging at most k points.
nodes.evidence: False for every fixed k: P_n's two solutions differ in all n rows (n = 5–11). With rotations of up to 4 points, 302 of 306 arrangements are disconnected at n = 10.

nodes.title: Starting lemma: Landau ⇒ parity test
nodes.intuition: The parity test asks: decide for each stone whether its point goes in an odd or an even row, so that the numbers match, and then check that a fractional solution exists using only the allowed cells. Any real solution supplies such a choice, so the test is weaker than having a solution. It can be checked by linear programming once the choice is made, which is what makes it a usable invariant. Claim: every valid square board passes.

pics.cap: 1 4 2 5 3 gives a choice: 0, −1, −2 in odd rows; +2, +1 in even rows

nodes.statement: If D satisfies Landau, the square n×n board with diagonals D passes the parity test: there is a choice a(d) ∈ {odd, even} for each d ∈ D such that the parity counts match and the fractional placement using only cells (r, c) with r ≡ a(c − r) exists.
nodes.evidence: Holds for n ≤ 12, tight cuts included, but checked via real solutions, so no evidence beyond the conjecture. Only the all-same-parity D has a unique working choice.

nodes.title: Rule: parity from a stone's position
nodes.intuition: The simplest kind of parity choice reads a stone's parity off its own mark and its rank. Claim: one such rule works for every arrangement.
nodes.statement: There is a function f such that for every valid D, the choice a(d) = f(d, rank of d in D) passes the parity test.
nodes.example:
D = {−1, 0, 1} forces a(0) = odd, but D = {−2, 0, 2} forces a(0) = even,
and 0 has rank 2 in both.
nodes.evidence: Fails at n = 3 (example). Also fail: rules from parity-class rank (n = 6), local Landau slack (n = 7), alternating within parity classes (n = 6), every function of 4 binary local features (n ≤ 6).

nodes.title: Minimal moves keep the parity test passing
nodes.intuition: The parity test can be carried along minimal moves like 'has a solution', but it is a weaker property, so the step might be easier. Claim: a minimal move never breaks the parity test.

pics.cap: Before and after a move, each with a passing choice

nodes.statement: If D passes the parity test and D → D′ is a minimal move, then D′ passes the parity test.
nodes.evidence: True for n ≤ 12, since every valid D passes there (starting lemma); no direct argument yet.

nodes.title: Carry a parity choice across a move
nodes.intuition: Instead of finding a new parity choice after a move, keep the old one: the two moving stones share a parity and pass it on to their new marks. Claim: some working choice always carries over like this.
nodes.statement: For every minimal move a, b → a+1, b−1 from a D that passes the parity test, some working choice for D with equal values on a and b becomes a working choice for D′ after giving a+1 and b−1 that value and keeping all other values.
nodes.evidence: Holds for the moves with nothing between the movers, n ≤ 11 (from solutions) and n ≤ 10 (from the LP). Not yet checked for general minimal moves. 'Every working choice carries over' fails at n = 6 (D = (−4,−3,0,1,2,4), x = −3).

nodes.title: Peeling lemma: some top-row cell keeps the test
nodes.intuition: Peeling places one point in the top row and deletes everything it uses, leaving a smaller board with a hole where the column was. The invariant is the parity test, which is weaker than 'has a solution' and checkable, so this is a genuine step rather than the conjecture in disguise. In the example, the top row can use diagonal +1 or +2; +1 runs dry two rows later, while +2 leaves a board that fills. Claim: every board passing the parity test has some top-row cell that keeps it passing.

pics.cap: Top row on +2 (not +1); the peeled board still fills

nodes.statement: Every board with rows 1…m and any m columns that passes the parity test has a top-row cell whose peel (delete its row, its column and its diagonal) leaves a board that still passes.
nodes.evidence: Some top-row cell always peels: rows 1…m with h ≤ 3 holes, m ≤ 7, and h = 2, m = 8. The peel can always keep the same parity choice (m ≤ 7, h ≤ 3), but not every passing choice works.

nodes.title: Parity test is exact on boards with holes
nodes.intuition: With holes, two new things go wrong for the plain fractional test. A row can have no usable cell at all (left picture: every column is odd, so row 1 only sees even diagonals). And a fractional solution can put half of each stone in an odd row and half in an even row (right picture). Claim: choosing parities first removes every such cheat, so passing the parity test is the same as having a placement.

pics.cap: Two holes: row 1 has no cell on a diagonal of D
Fractional but not real: every diagonal split ½ odd, ½ even

nodes.statement: A board with rows 1…m and any m columns has a placement ⇔ it passes the parity test.
nodes.evidence: Exact on all tested boards: 2 holes up to m = 10, 3 up to m = 9, 4 up to m = 7. General row sets only up to m = 5.

nodes.title: Rule: a fixed top-row choice
nodes.intuition: The obvious ways to choose the top row's point. Claim: one of them always works.

pics.cap: Largest (+3) and smallest (0) both fail; only +2 works

nodes.statement: At least one of these always keeps the parity test passing: (a) the top-row cell with the largest diagonal, (b) the smallest, (c) the largest weight in the fractional solution.
nodes.evidence: (a), (b) fail at m = 4 (picture); (c) fails at m = 6, h = 3, where the restricted fractional solution is all ½.

nodes.title: Rule: a weight-1 corner for a fixed parity choice
nodes.intuition: A cell with weight 1 in a fractional solution uses up its row, column and diagonal, so peeling it keeps the rest of that solution. Claim: every passing choice has such a cell at some vertex.
nodes.statement: For every passing parity choice, the restricted fractional polytope has a vertex with some cell of weight exactly 1.
nodes.evidence: False: m = 6, h = 3, columns {1,3,4,7,8,9}, D = {−3,−1,2,3,4,6} has a unique all-½ solution for one passing choice. For some choice a weight-1 vertex always existed in tests, but that version is equivalent to the peeling lemma.

nodes.title: Bad peels are forced contradictions
nodes.intuition: Forced moves: if some row, column or diagonal has only one usable cell, the point must go there, which deletes more cells and may force the next point. In the example, taking diagonal 0 in the top row forces +3 into cell (3, 6), and then row 2 has no usable cell left. Claim: a peel is bad exactly when, for every parity choice, the counts are off or forced moves run into an empty line.

pics.cap: Forced: +3 at (3, 6). Then row 2 has no usable cell

nodes.statement: Peel a top-row cell e of a board passing the parity test, leaving board P. Then P fails the parity test ⇔ for every parity choice a of P, either the parity counts don't match, or forced-move propagation on the a-restricted P empties some row, column or diagonal. (Propagation: while some row, column or diagonal has exactly one usable cell, place a point there and delete its lines.)
nodes.evidence: Exact on all tested boards: m ≤ 7 with up to 4 holes, m = 8 with up to 3. Propagation alone (no parity) explains 96–99% of bad cells; parity first matters at m = 7. A real placement survives forced moves, so the rule never wrongly calls a cell bad. The raw LP certificates are a zoo (dozens of sign patterns, weights up to 6).

nodes.title: Some top-row cell never sets off a dead end
nodes.intuition: This is the peeling lemma with the LP taken out: instead of a fractional solution, we only need one top-row cell whose forced consequences never run dry. On the same board as the 'bad peels' example, taking +3 in the top row forces every remaining point one after another, and nothing runs dry. Claim: every board passing the parity test has such a cell.

pics.cap: Every remaining point is forced, and no line runs dry

nodes.statement: Every board with rows 1…m passing the parity test has a top-row cell e and a parity choice a for the peeled board such that the parity counts match and forced-move propagation on the a-restricted peeled board never empties a row, column or diagonal.

nodes.title: G1: the sum test is exact with one missing column
nodes.intuition: Place the largest stone in the top row first. Deleting that row and its column leaves a smaller board with a hole where the column was. On such one-hole boards, Landau's test still makes sense if 'the k leftmost columns' skips over the hole. Claim: on boards with one missing column, this adjusted test is exact.

pics.cap: +2 goes in row 1, column 3; column 3 becomes a hole and the rest fills

nodes.statement: Rows 1…m, columns {1…m+1} ∖ {c}, t_k = d_k + m − k: a placement exists ⇔ Σ_{i≤k} t_i ≥ C(k,2) + max(0, k+1−c) for all k, with equality at k = m.
nodes.evidence: Sufficiency verified by computer for m ≤ 15 (Devin).

nodes.title: The sum test is exact with two or more holes
nodes.intuition: Peeling rows one at a time creates more holes, so G1 would follow if the sum test kept working. Claim: it works with any number of holes.

pics.cap: Passes the sum test, but row 1 sees only even diagonals

nodes.statement: On boards with rows 1…m and two or more missing columns, the Landau-type sum test implies a placement.
nodes.evidence: Fails from m = 3: rows 1–3, columns {1,3,5}, D = {−1,1,3} (picture).

nodes.title: Edge peeling stays inside one-hole boards
nodes.intuition: Another route to G1: always peel an edge line chosen so that the board keeps at most one hole. Claim: some such class is closed under peeling and has an exact sum test.
nodes.statement: Some class of boards with at most one hole is closed under peeling a suitable edge row or column, and the sum test is exact on it.
nodes.example:
Stuck board: rows 1–4, columns {1,2,4,5}, D = {−2,−1,2,3}:
every peel leaves the class.
nodes.evidence: About 19% of boards get stuck at m = 8; enlargements of the class fail too.

nodes.title: Plain fractional test is exact with holes
nodes.intuition: Without choosing parities first. Claim: the plain fractional test is already exact with holes.
nodes.statement: On boards with missing columns, a fractional placement implies a real one.
nodes.evidence: First failure at m = 6: columns {1,2,5,6,7,8}, D = {−3,−2,0,2,5,6} has a unique all-½ fractional solution (the parity claim's second picture).

nodes.title: Li–Yao: the fractional version is true
nodes.intuition: Allow points to be split into fractions spread over several cells. Claim: Landau's condition is always enough for such a fractional solution.

pics.cap: {−1, 0, +1}: every row, column and diagonal sums to 1 using halves

nodes.statement: If s satisfies Landau, there is a doubly stochastic matrix supported on the diagonals of D in which each diagonal of D sums to 1.
nodes.proof: Li–Yao / Li–Liu–Yao: by LP duality, a doubly stochastic matrix with these diagonal sums exists iff a family of weighted inequalities I(w) holds for all weights w ≥ 0; an induction on the weights reduces every I(w) to Landau's finitely many inequalities.

nodes.title: Capacity bound
nodes.intuition: Give each allowed diagonal d a weight x_d and fill the board in every possible way using allowed diagonals, letting stones pile up on the same mark. Each filling contributes the product of the weights it uses; the total is the polynomial P. Fillings that use every weight once are the solutions, so the number of solutions W is the coefficient of the product of all weights. Divide P by that product and push the weights to make the result small: the solutions always contribute exactly W, while piled-up fillings can be pushed down. The smallest value reached is the capacity; it is positive exactly when a fractional solution exists. Claim: the number of solutions is never below n!/nⁿ times the capacity.

pics.cap: {−1, 0, +1}: each cell carries the weight of its diagonal

nodes.statement: W(D) ≥ (n!/nⁿ)·cap(P_D), where P_D(x) = per(M) with M_ij = x_{j−i} if j − i ∈ D (else 0), and cap(P_D) = inf_{x>0} P_D(x)/∏_d x_d.
nodes.example:
Weights on {−1, 0, +1}:
  x₀  x₁  ·
  x₋₁ x₀  x₁
  ·   x₋₁ x₀
Fillings: 123 → x₀³ (three stones on mark 0)
          132 → x₀x₁x₋₁ (a solution)
          213 → x₁x₋₁x₀ (a solution)
P = x₀³ + 2·x₋₁x₀x₁, so W = 2.
P/(x₋₁x₀x₁) = x₀²/(x₋₁x₁) + 2 → smallest value 2: cap = 2.
Bound: W ≥ (6/27)·2 ≈ 0.44. True: W = 2.
nodes.evidence: Holds for every no-tight-cut D with n ≤ 11 (n ≤ 8 Devin; n = 9–11 exhaustive). The slack W·nⁿ/(n!·cap) is at least 13.8, 17.2, 18.0 at n = 9, 10, 11 and grows with n; the worst cases are near-regular arrangements with many solutions, not P_n. Along P_n (W = 2) the slack grows like e^{0.21n} through n = 20.

nodes.title: P_D is real stable or log-concave
nodes.intuition: Known proofs that a coefficient is at least a fixed fraction of the capacity need the polynomial to be real stable, or at least log-concave on positive inputs. Claim: ours is.
nodes.statement: P_D is real stable, or at least log-concave on the positive orthant (or Lorentzian), so the Gurvits / Anari–Oveis Gharan–Vinzant coefficient bounds apply.
nodes.example:
D = {−1, 0, 1}: P = x₀³ + 2·x₋₁x₀x₁.
At (x₋₁, x₀, x₁) = (½, 1, ½), along (1, 0, 1),
the second derivative of log P is 8/9 > 0: not log-concave.
nodes.evidence: Fails at n = 3 (example) and for every no-tight-cut D with n ≤ 7: not log-concave, not Lorentzian, support not M-convex.

nodes.title: Gurvits' one-variable step
nodes.intuition: Gurvits' proof removes one variable at a time and shows the capacity never drops by more than a fixed factor per step; chaining the steps gives the bound. Claim: the same per-step bound holds for our polynomials in some order.
nodes.statement: In some order, removing one variable at a time (q = ∂P/∂x_d at x_d = 0) lowers the capacity by at most a factor ((k−1)/k)^{k−1} (k = deg_{x_d}), or by at most a fixed constant c > 0, at every step.
nodes.example:
P₅ = {−3, −2, 0, 2, 3}: removing x₀ first gives
q = a²d² + 2abcd + 2b²c²  (a, b, c, d = x₋₃, x₋₂, x₂, x₃),
cap(q) = 2 + 2√2; removing any next variable leaves 2·(the rest),
losing a factor √2 − 1 where Gurvits allows ½.
nodes.evidence: Gurvits' factor fails at n = 5 for P₅ in every order. The best constant per step shrinks: 0.5, 0.39, 0.33, 0.33, 0.26, 0.22 for n = 4–9, always worst at P_n.

nodes.title: Saturation with repeats allowed
nodes.intuition: If every whole-number point of the fractional region were realised, Li–Yao would immediately give a solution. Claim: it is, even when marks may hold several stones.
nodes.statement: Every lattice point of the polytope of all permutation x-rays (repeated diagonals allowed) is the x-ray of some permutation.
nodes.example:
n = 12: e = {−8, −7, −3⁵, 1, 7³, 8} is the average of two x-rays,
but no permutation has x-ray e.
nodes.evidence: Holds for n ≤ 11, fails at n = 12 (example).

nodes.title: Round any fractional solution
nodes.intuition: Start from a fractional solution and clean it up. Claim: any fractional solution can be rounded to a real one with the same diagonals.
nodes.statement: Every doubly stochastic matrix with a binary x-ray can be rounded to a permutation matrix with the same x-ray.
nodes.evidence: Li–Liu–Yao Sec. 5: a 5×5 doubly stochastic matrix with entries ½ and x-ray (0,0,1,1,1,1,0,0) can't be rounded keeping its x-ray (a permutation with that x-ray exists anyway).

nodes.title: General three-way-table version
nodes.intuition: A broader version of the problem, with three families of lines in place of rows, columns and diagonals. Claim: integrality holds there too.
nodes.statement: Integer version of Li–Liu–Yao's Conj. 5.3: every triangular contingency table problem with binary marginals that has a fractional solution has an integer one.
nodes.evidence: False at n = 112 (Prop 5.4): binary marginals whose table is unique and has a ½ entry. So a proof must use the geometry of the square board.

nodes.title: Signed solution counts are nonzero
nodes.intuition: Polynomial-method proofs (Alon–Tarsi) show existence by showing a coefficient is nonzero; here the natural coefficient is the signed count of solutions. Claim: it never vanishes.
nodes.statement: For every valid no-tight-cut D, Σ_{witnesses π of D} sign(π) ≠ 0.
nodes.evidence: Vanishes for some valid no-tight-cut D at n = 4–6.

nodes.title: Global counting forces every arrangement to be hit
nodes.intuition: A counting proof would build many objects (here: all permutations with distinct diagonals), count them, count the repeats, and conclude there are too many for any arrangement to be left out. Cauchy–Schwarz says the number of arrangements that get at least one witness is at least (total)² / (sum of squared counts), so if that exceeded A_n − 1, every arrangement would be hit. Claim: the counts are spread evenly enough for this to work.
nodes.statement: For every n, (Σ_D W(D))² / Σ_D W(D)² > A_n − 1, where the sums run over valid D of size n and A_n is the number of valid D.
nodes.example:
n = 5: 9 arrangements, 23 witnesses, Σ W² = 77:
23² / 77 ≈ 6.9, not above 8.
n = 9: 490 arrangements, ΣW = 12657, ratio ≈ 208.
nodes.evidence: False for every n checked: the ratio is 6.9, 16.4, 34.7, 92, 208 against A_n − 1 = 8, 21, 58, 166, 489 for n = 5–9, so it covers well under half. The counts are very uneven (P_n has 2 witnesses, others hundreds), so any global count with repeats loses. A counting proof has to give a lower bound for each arrangement separately, as the capacity and move-ratio claims do.

nodes.title: Every score sequence has a tournament δ accepts
nodes.intuition: Davis–Schroeder turn each solution into a tournament with the same scores, and give a condition on a tournament under which the process can be reversed to produce a solution. Tournaments with given valid scores are easy to build (Landau's theorem), so it would be enough to find, for each score sequence, one tournament satisfying their condition. The accepted tournaments turn out to be exactly those that come from solutions, so this is close to a restatement; the hope is a natural canonical tournament. Claim: every valid score sequence has an accepted tournament.
nodes.statement: For every valid score sequence s there is a tournament with scores s on which Davis–Schroeder's reverse map δ is defined (then δ of it is a witness).
nodes.evidence: The accepted tournaments are exactly the images of solutions (checked n ≤ 6), so the claim is equivalent to the conjecture in that range. Accepted fraction drops to 2% at n = 8.

nodes.title: Rule: the most-upsets tournament
nodes.intuition: A canonical choice: among tournaments with the right scores, take one with as many upsets as possible. Claim: one of those is always accepted.
nodes.statement: For every valid score sequence s, some tournament with scores s and the maximum possible number of upsets is accepted by δ.
nodes.evidence: Holds for n ≤ 8; fails at n = 9 for s = (1,2,3,3,4,5,5,6,7) (accepted reach 10 upsets, the maximum is 11). Staircase, rotational and Havel–Hakimi tournaments fail earlier.

nodes.title: Tested greedy placement rules
nodes.intuition: Landau's theorem for tournaments has step-by-step constructions. Claim: one of these step-by-step placements never gets stuck.
nodes.statement: One of the 92 tested greedy rules (Havel–Hakimi style, fixed diagonal orders, least-damage, row-by-row urgency, most-constrained-first) finds a witness without backtracking for every valid no-tight-cut D.
nodes.example:
n = 5, D = {−3, −2, 0, 2, 3}: a few placements can leave rows {2,3,4},
columns {1,3,5}, diagonals {−2,0,2}, all usable only in row 3.
nodes.evidence: All 92 fail by n ≤ 10; the best fails 0.5–0.9% at n = 11–13.

nodes.title: Solutions are walks on pairs of Young diagrams
nodes.intuition: Number the rows from the bottom. Then a stone on the k-th smallest diagonal sits in a cell whose row number plus column number is a fixed target, and the targets increase with k. Place the stones in that order. After k stones, all that matters for the future is which rows and which columns are used. With no drift these would be rows 1…k and columns 1…k. The slack σ_k says exactly how far the used rows and used columns together stick out above that, so the two sets are described by two Young diagrams with σ_k boxes in total. A solution is a walk on such pairs that starts and ends at the empty pair. Nothing in the rules for one step mentions n. Claim: solutions are exactly these walks, and when the slack stays below a fixed bound, one finite machine decides solvability for boards of every size.
nodes.statement: Sort D and put e_k = s_k − (k−1), σ_k = e_1 + … + e_k (the Landau slack of the first k stones). Witnesses of D correspond one-to-one to sequences of pairs of partitions (λ_k, μ_k), k = 0…n, with (λ_0, μ_0) = (λ_n, μ_n) = (∅, ∅), |λ_k| + |μ_k| = σ_k, in which step k adds one bead to each partition at offsets u and v with u + v = e_k. The allowed steps do not depend on k or n. If all σ_k ≤ B, only finitely many pairs can occur, so whether D has a witness is decided by a finite automaton A_B that reads e_1, e_2, … and is the same for every n.
nodes.example:
The board above, rows numbered from the bottom, stones in order of diagonal:
(row, column) = (1,2), (2,3), (5,1), (3,4), (4,5); row + column = 3, 5, 6, 7, 9.
Used rows / columns after each stone, as (rows diagram, columns diagram):
{1} / {2}: (∅, 1)   {1,2} / {2,3}: (∅, 1+1)   {1,2,5} / {1,2,3}: (2, ∅)
{1,2,3,5} / {1,2,3,4}: (1, ∅)   all / all: (∅, ∅).
Box counts 1, 2, 2, 1, 0 are the slacks.
nodes.refs: agents/interface/README.md §1; check_walks.py (walk count = number of witnesses, all valid D, n ≤ 8)
nodes.proof: Number rows from the bottom, r′ = n+1−r. A point on diagonal d = c − r has r′ + c = d + n + 1, so the k-th smallest diagonal needs r′ + c = b_k := d_k + n + 1 = 2k + e_k. A witness is a pair of bijections ρ, γ: {1…n} → {1…n} with ρ(k) + γ(k) = b_k. Let R_k = ρ({1…k}), C_k = γ({1…k}), and for a k-set X let exc(X) = ΣX − k(k+1)/2 ≥ 0. Then exc(R_k) + exc(C_k) = Σ_{i≤k} b_i − k(k+1) = σ_k. A k-set X = {x_1 < … < x_k} with excess j is the partition of j with parts x_i − i, so (R_k, C_k) is a pair of partitions with σ_k boxes in total; it starts and ends empty. Step k adds row k + u and column k + v with u + v = e_k, and whether a row or column is free depends only on the partitions and on u, v, not on k or n (n only enters through 'row ≤ n', which holds automatically because the final excess is 0). Conversely any such sequence of sets gives ρ and γ. If σ_k ≤ B then each excess is ≤ B, so a k-set contains {1…k−B} and is contained in {1…k+B}: finitely many states, and the transition rule is the same for all k.

nodes.title: Bounded slack: one finite machine per bound
nodes.intuition: The slack measures how far an arrangement is from the start. P_n is the family with slack 1 everywhere, and it needed its own formula. This card slices the whole problem by slack instead of by board size: for a fixed bound there are arrangements of every size, but only finitely many interface states, so the question for that bound is a finite check. Each bound settled is a theorem about all n at once. A proof for every bound needs a description of which interface states are reachable after a given prefix; the red cards below are the simple descriptions that fail. What the machine shows: after a few stones with e_k = 0 every pair of diagrams of the right size is reachable, and what matters is only the part of the word since that last happened. Claim: for every bound, the machine accepts every valid word.
nodes.statement: For every B ≥ 1, the automaton A_B accepts every valid no-tight-cut word with all slacks ≤ B. Equivalently: for every B, every valid D of every size whose Landau slacks are all ≤ B has a witness.
nodes.example:
B = 1: the only words are e = (1, 0, …, 0, −1), which is P_n.
The machine has 3 states and accepts all of them: P_n is solvable for every n.
nodes.evidence: Settled for B ≤ 16 by complete search of A_B (see the card for B = 16). Open for B ≥ 17, where only n ≤ 22 is known. The statement about stones with e_k = 0 was checked for B ≤ 8: from every reachable set of the machine after which a letter 0 is allowed, at most 7 letters 0 lead to the set of all pairs. From a single interface state this is false (at slack 1 the two states just alternate).

nodes.title: Every arrangement with slack at most 16 is solvable
nodes.intuition: The slack of a cut is the total drift of the stones to its left. The largest slack of an arrangement of size n is about n²/8, so small boards have small slack, but so do arrangements of any size that stay close to the start. For slack up to 16 the interface machine has a few thousand states, and a program can run through all of them. Claim: every arrangement of any size whose slacks never exceed 16 has a solution.
nodes.statement: For every n, every valid D whose Landau slacks σ_k are all ≤ 16 has a witness.
nodes.example:
P_n has slack 1 at every cut. A minimal move raises the slack by 1 at the cuts between its two stones,
so P_n followed by any 15 minimal moves is covered, for every n.
Every D with n ≤ 11 has slack ≤ 16.
nodes.evidence: Not a sample: the automaton A_16 (22,358 reachable states after determinising, 11 s, 0.94 GB) accepts every valid word, and by the interface card this covers every n. It is listed as empirical only because the finite check is done by a program. Three implementations give the same verdict (Python for B ≤ 8, two C++ programs for B ≤ 12), and the step rule was compared with brute force on all 6,742 multisets with repeats for n ≤ 8, including the 39 with no solution. B = 17 was not done: the program packs a state into 64 bits, which stops at B = 16, and the search would also need more than the 7 GB available. Does not depend on the conjecture at any size. Recheck: g++ -O2 -o slack_dfa slack_dfa.cpp && ./slack_dfa 16.

nodes.title: Alive sets are closed under moving boxes down
nodes.intuition: An induction over the slack bound needs a description of which hole states are still alive after a prefix. The simplest hope is an order-theoretic shape, like Landau's own condition: if a state is alive, so is every 'more spread out' one. Claim: alive sets have that shape.
nodes.statement: For every valid prefix, the set of alive interface states (λ, μ) is closed under replacing λ or μ by a diagram it dominates (equivalently, moving a box to a lower row), or under the reverse; the same for the combined diagram of rows and columns interleaved.
nodes.evidence: False in every version. With slack ≤ 6, 100 distinct alive sets occur: all are symmetric under swapping rows and columns, but only 14 are closed downward and 14 upward under dominance, and only 20 are intervals in the interleaved form. Example at slack 5: with no row holes, the column diagrams 41, 32, 311, 221 are alive and 5, 2111, 11111 are dead — the middle of the order survives, both extremes die.

nodes.title: One hole pattern is at least as good as another
nodes.intuition: If some hole patterns were simply better than others, a reachable set could be replaced by its best members, and comparing two words would come down to comparing single patterns. That would give alive sets a shape (everything below the best ones) and a way to prove that one word is easier than another. Claim: some hole pattern is at least as good as a different one, move by move.
nodes.statement: There is a pair of different interface states t, t′ of the same slack, not mirror images, such that t′ can answer every move of t: for every legal next letter, every successor of t is again answered by some successor of t′, and t′ is empty whenever t is.
nodes.evidence: False for every state of slack ≤ 7: among the 434 states with slack ≤ 8 the only comparable pairs are a state and its mirror image. Every hole pattern has continuations that no other single pattern can follow, so a comparison of reachable sets has to use several states together. Recheck: python3 sim.py 8 (3 seconds).

nodes.title: Alive sets are boxes
nodes.intuition: Alive sets are not closed in either direction under moving boxes, because both very deep and very spread-out hole patterns die. The next simplest hope is a two-sided rule: alive means fitting inside a box, not too wide and not too tall. Claim: the alive set is always exactly the states that fit in its bounding box.
nodes.statement: For every valid prefix, an interface state (λ, μ) of the current slack is alive exactly when its four dimensions (longest row and number of rows of λ and of μ) are at most the largest values of those dimensions among alive states.
nodes.evidence: Exact for only 20 of the 100 alive sets with slack ≤ 6 and 33 of 363 with slack ≤ 8. Worse, no rule using only these four dimensions (plus the split of the slack between rows and columns) works: at slack 8, with no row holes, column pattern 4 2 2 is alive while 4 3 1 is dead, and the two have the same width, height and size. Adding the number of odd parts separates every case to slack 8, but only because those features then identify every state uniquely, so that says nothing.

nodes.title: Online rule: place each stone before seeing the next diagonal
nodes.intuition: The simplest proof in diagonal order would be a rule with no lookahead. Claim: such a rule exists.
nodes.statement: There is a rule that places the stone of the k-th smallest diagonal knowing only n and the k smallest diagonals, and that completes a witness for every valid D.
nodes.example: n = 8: whatever the rule does, an adversary who reveals the diagonals one at a time can steer to a valid D on which the rule is stuck. No two arrangements suffice for this; the adversary needs a branching strategy.
nodes.evidence: Exhaustive game search: a rule exists for n ≤ 7 and for no n from 8 to 11. On the automaton: exists for B ≤ 2, not for B = 3…8.
nodes.refs: agents/interface/online_fixed_n.py, online_check.py (independent recheck, n ≤ 9), online_game.py, online_cex.py

nodes.title: Invariant from the slack and the last few diagonals
nodes.intuition: An induction along the word needs an invariant: a set of interface states guaranteed reachable. Claim: the invariant can be read off from the current slack and a bounded window of recent diagonals.
nodes.statement: For some L with 1 ≤ L ≤ 4 there is a family I(σ, e_{k−L+1}, …, e_k) of nonempty sets of interface states such that every prefix with that slack and those last L letters reaches every state of I, and each step maps I onto a superset of the next I.
nodes.example: Window of 2 letters, arrangements with slack ≤ 5: the largest family satisfying the step condition is empty, for instance at slack 1 after the letters (0, 0).
nodes.evidence: Largest such family computed exactly inside slack ≤ B: a window of L = 1 letter works only for B ≤ 2, L = 2 only for B ≤ 4, L = 3 only for B ≤ 8, L = 4 only for B ≤ 13. So no window of at most 4 letters works for all D, and the window needed grows with the slack bound. Windows of 5 or more letters were not run to failure. Replacing the window by the last letter plus a capped counter (length, largest slack so far, sum of slacks, largest letter, steps since the last rise) fails from B = 4.

nodes.title: Counting: the two halves must meet at the middle cut
nodes.intuition: D has a solution exactly when some interface state at a cut can be reached both from the left and from the right. If the two reachable sets together had more elements than there are states, they would have to share one. Claim: at the middle cut they always do.
nodes.statement: For every valid no-tight-cut D of size n and k = ⌊n/2⌋: |F_k| + |G_k| > N_k, where F_k is the set of interface states reachable by placing the k smallest diagonals, G_k the set reachable backwards by placing the n − k largest, and N_k the number of all interface states at that cut.
nodes.example: n = 15, D = {−9, …, 0, 2, 8, 10, 12, 13}, cut after 7 stones: the two sets together have 0.973 times the number of states (they still meet).
nodes.evidence: True for every D with n ≤ 14 (exhaustive; the smallest ratio falls steadily: 2, 1.75, 1.6, 1.56, 1.47, 1.41, 1.33, 1.23, 1.14, 1.10, 1.03 for n = 4…14). Fails at n = 15 (example).

nodes.title: Each diagonal used at most twice
nodes.intuition: The conjecture asks for one stone per chosen diagonal. Allow a diagonal to be chosen twice, keeping the same Landau sums. With three stones on one diagonal Landau is no longer enough, and with five even a fractional solution is not enough. With at most two, no failure has turned up. A stronger statement can be easier to prove by induction, because steps may pass through arrangements with a doubled diagonal: for example, swapping two adjacent columns of any solution moves one stone up one diagonal and one stone down one, which often creates a double. Claim: Landau is sufficient whenever no diagonal is used more than twice.
nodes.statement: Let d_1 ≤ … ≤ d_n be integers in which no value occurs more than twice, with Σ_{i≤k} (d_i + n − i) ≥ C(k,2) for all k and equality at k = n. Then some permutation has exactly these diagonals, with these multiplicities.
nodes.example:
n = 4, diagonals {−1, −1, 1, 1}: the permutation 2 1 4 3 has them.
n = 6, diagonals {−2, −2, −2, 2, 2, 2} (Landau holds): no permutation. Rows 1, 2 need diagonal +2 and rows 5, 6 need −2, and both pairs land in columns 3, 4.
nodes.evidence: Exhaustive for n ≤ 15 (174,292,169 multisets at n = 15, no failure), and for every n when all slacks are ≤ 12 (automaton with repeats, 207,436 states). Among all multisets passing Landau, those with no solution number 1, 6, 32, 145, 634 for n = 6…10 and every one has a diagonal used at least three times. The fractional test stays exact for all multisets up to n = 11 and first fails at n = 12 with a diagonal used five times (the saturation card's example). Does not depend on the conjecture. Recheck: g++ -O2 -o twice twice.cpp && ./twice 13 2.

nodes.title: Each diagonal used at most three times
nodes.intuition: Claim: Landau stays sufficient with triples.
nodes.statement: The same statement with 'no value occurs more than three times'.
nodes.example: n = 6, diagonals {−2, −2, −2, 2, 2, 2}: Landau holds, no permutation.
nodes.evidence: Smallest failure is n = 6 (unique there).

nodes.title: Pairs with prescribed sums, any parity
nodes.intuition: A solution is the same as splitting {1, …, 2n} into pairs with the odd sums 2(d_k + n) + 1: an odd sum forces one odd number (a row) and one even number (a column). Dropping 'odd' gives a more symmetric puzzle with no board in it. Claim: the Landau-type condition is sufficient for any prescribed sums.
nodes.statement: If c_1 < … < c_m are integers with Σ_{i≤j} c_i ≥ j(2j+1) for all j and equality at j = m, then {1, …, 2m} can be split into pairs whose sums are c_1, …, c_m.
nodes.example: m = 4, sums (4, 8, 10, 14): no pairing of {1, …, 8}. Even sums pair odd with odd and even with even; the odd numbers can make {4,12}, {6,10} or {8,8} and the even ones {6,14}, {8,12} or {10,10}.
nodes.evidence: With all sums odd this is the conjecture (no failure, m ≤ 8). With even sums allowed: 1 of 37 fails at m = 4, 1026 of 50944 at m = 8.

nodes.title: Every stone within one mark of evenly spaced
nodes.intuition: The evenly spaced arrangement −(n−1), −(n−3), …, n−1 is solved by the anti-diagonal. Move each stone at most one mark, keeping Landau: this is the smallest family of arrangements in which the Landau slack is unbounded, so it is not covered by the bounded-slack machine, yet every letter of the word is −1, 0 or +1. It is a test case for any induction along the word: here the set of interface states that every prefix is guaranteed to reach depends on the slack alone. Claim: all these arrangements are solvable.
nodes.statement: Let e_1, …, e_n ∈ {−1, 0, +1} have all partial sums ≥ 0 and total 0, in any order. Then some permutation has the diagonals d_k = 2k − n − 1 + e_k (as a multiset; a value occurs twice exactly where a + is followed by a −).
nodes.example: n = 5, word + + 0 − −: diagonals {−3, −1, 0, 1, 3}. Witness 2 5 3 1 4.
nodes.evidence: All 5,798 words at n = 11 and all shorter ones have a witness. Inside slack ≤ 10 there is a family F(σ) of interface states, depending on the slack σ only, with F(σ+e) ⊆ step_e(F(σ)) for each letter e; its sizes are 2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 80 for σ = 1…7, and it needs states with 3 advanced lines from slack 7 on. No description of F was found; the smallest such family (integer program, slack ≤ 7) is forced up to slack 3 and shows no pattern. For letters in {−2, …, 2} the slack plus the last two letters already fails at slack 5. Witnesses must move stones far: the least displacement max |row − k| is ≤ 1 for exactly 2^(n−1) words and reaches 3 at n = 8.
nodes.refs: agents/interface/letters_notes.md, letters_ansatz.py (n ≤ 11), letters_sigma.py, letters_Fclass.py, letters_min.py, letters.py

nodes.title: Zigzag chain from every solution
nodes.intuition: Every word of the parent card is built from single zeros and blocks + M − with M shorter, so one lemma would finish the induction: a solution of M can be turned into a solution of + M −. The natural repair passes a one-unit shortage from stone to stone. Claim: this chain always ends at the last stone.
nodes.statement: Let M be a word as in the parent card, W any witness of M, and add corner stones to get a witness of 0 M 0. Move stone 1 up one row; the stone it displaces is then one short and is moved one column right; continue, alternating rows and columns (or columns first). For every M and W the chain reaches the last stone, giving a witness of + M −.
nodes.example: n = 10, M = + 0 − + + 0 − −: from 4 of the 8 witnesses of M the chain returns to its starting position after 28 moves without ever touching the last stone.
nodes.evidence: True for every witness of every M up to n = 9. At n = 10 it fails for 4 witnesses of one word; the other 4 work. What survives: start only from witnesses that this induction built (direct sums and chain results). That class is non-empty for every word with n ≤ 13 (41,835 words at n = 13; the chain loops in 1,096 of about 200,000 runs, never for all witnesses of a word). No simple choice of witness (least displacement, fewest inversions, lexicographic) always works. The chain never gets stuck at the border: by the leapfrog card its only failure is a closed loop.

nodes.title: The chain runs in rounds
nodes.intuition: The chain looks like one long walk, but it has a simple large-scale shape. The mark climbs through the blocks of M one after another. Each block either lets it through to the next block or sends it back, and a mark that is sent back retraces its steps all the way to the bottom stone, repairing every block below on the way. So a run is a sequence of rounds, started alternately by a row move and a column move; each failed round changes exactly one block. Whether a block lets the mark through depends only on the block's position and on whether the mark enters by a row or a column move.
nodes.statement: Let M = U_1 … U_k, each U_i a single 0 or a block + M′ −, and take any witness of each U_i, placed as a direct sum between two corner stones (U_0 and U_{k+1}). Run the zigzag chain of the card 'Zigzag chain from every solution'. Then: (a) the mark only passes between stones of the same U_i or of neighbouring ones; (b) whenever it passes down from U_j to U_{j−1} it goes on down to the bottom stone, undoing every move of the current round outside U_j, so that only U_j has changed; (c) the bottom stone then makes its other move. If U_j in position q sends back a mark that entered by a row move and ends in position q′, then in position q′ it sends back a mark entering by a row move and ends in q; the same for column moves.
nodes.example: M = (+ 0 −)(+ + 0 − −), n = 10. The witness of + 0 − built rows-first always lets the mark through and hands it on by a column move; the one built columns-first hands it on by a row move. A witness of + + 0 − − built rows-first lets a row move through and sends a column move back. So the chain loops exactly when both blocks were built with the same first move.
nodes.evidence: Proof: let I_i be the rows (= columns) of U_i. By induction on the moves, below the marked block each boundary has exactly one pair of neighbouring lines exchanged (the two rows or the two columns at the boundary), and above it nothing has moved; so a move either stays inside a block, or exchanges the two lines at a boundary going up, or undoes that exchange going down. When the mark comes down into U_{j−1}, no stone of U_{j−1} or below has moved since the mark left, so the stone that receives it is the one that passed it up, back in its earlier place, and its next move is of the kind by which it first received the mark; that move is its own inverse, so it undoes the earlier one, and so on down to the bottom stone. Checked on 1,705,474 chain runs (n ≤ 15): no exception.

nodes.title: Every block lets each kind of move through
nodes.intuition: By the card 'The chain runs in rounds', the first round reaches the top if every block lets the mark through. A single stone always does. So if every block had, for each kind of entering move, a witness that lets it through, one could choose the witnesses from the bottom up and the first round would never fail. Because of the reflection that exchanges rows and columns, it is enough that some witness of the block lets some move through. Claim: such witnesses always exist.
nodes.statement: Let K be the class of witnesses built by direct sums and the zigzag chain (K(0) = one stone; K(+ M −) = all results of the chain from direct sums of members of K of the blocks of M). For every block B = + M − and for each kind of move m (row or column) there is a witness in K(B) which, placed between two corner stones, lets a mark that enters by m through to the top stone.
nodes.example: B = + + 0 − −: the witness built rows-first lets a row move through and sends a column move back; the one built columns-first does the opposite.
nodes.evidence: True for all 9,360 blocks of length ≤ 13 (69,907 distinct witnesses in K; 510 of them send both kinds of move back, first at length 10). The claim for B is about a second mark crossing the trail of the first, and is not an induction by itself: for + 0 … 0 − the second mark visits every third stone, so what a block does depends on its length mod 3.

nodes.title: Shortening induction: three ways to lengthen a solvable arrangement
nodes.intuition: Write an arrangement as its word: for each stone, from the lowest diagonal up, how far it is from its evenly spaced position. A run of letters falling by one each step, such as 2, 1, 0, −1, is a block of neighbouring diagonals. Three operations make a word one or two stones longer. PEAK replaces one stone at its evenly spaced place by three neighbouring diagonals 1, 0, −1. ZERO inserts a 0 between a 0 and a −1. RUN adds one stone to a block of neighbouring diagonals whose letters cross zero. Every arrangement except the evenly spaced one is produced from a shorter valid arrangement by one of the three (proved: look at the first negative letter; it is a −1 after a 0, and before that 0 stands a 0, which gives ZERO, or a 1, which gives PEAK or RUN on the whole block). The evenly spaced arrangement is solved by the anti-diagonal. So the conjecture is equivalent to: each operation keeps an arrangement solvable. The lab shows the chain for any arrangement up to n = 9. Claim: PEAK, ZERO and RUN each turn a solvable arrangement into a solvable one.
nodes.statement: For all letter strings x, y: if the word x u y is a valid arrangement with a solution, then x v y has a solution, for each of: PEAK u = (0), v = (1, 0, −1). ZERO u = (0, −1), v = (0, 0, −1). RUN(a, b), a, b ≥ 1, (a, b) ≠ (1, 1): v = (a, a−1, …, −b), u = (a−1, …, −(b−1)) with the letter a−b written twice.
nodes.example: P_4 = (1, 0, 0, −1) comes from (1, 0, −1) by ZERO, which comes from (0) by PEAK.
nodes.evidence: The reduction (every nonzero valid word is shortened to a valid word) is proved and checked on all 6,561 words of length ≤ 11 with slack ≤ 8. The claim itself follows from the conjecture, so tests of it say nothing new; what is needed is a proof of each operation. The natural stronger form, on whole sets of reachable hole patterns, is false (red child).

nodes.title: The three operations never lose a reachable hole pattern
nodes.intuition: The interface machine reads a word letter by letter and keeps the set of hole patterns it can reach.
