If the longer piece v reaches every hole pattern that the shorter piece u reaches, after every beginning x, then the operation keeps arrangements solvable, and this can be tested on the finite machine for each slack bound. It holds for every beginning with slack up to 12, and then breaks. Claim: after every legal beginning, the longer piece reaches every hole pattern the shorter piece reaches.
nodes.statement: F(x) = set of interface states reachable after the prefix x. For every legal prefix x: F(x 0) ⊆ F(x 1 0 −1), F(x −1) ⊆ F(x 0 −1), and F(x u) ⊆ F(x v) for every RUN(a, b).
nodes.example: RUN(2, 1) fails after x = (4, 3, 2, 1): two hole patterns are reached by x 1 1 0 and not by x 2 1 0 −1 (slack 13 on the way). ZERO fails after x = (2, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0), slack 14.
nodes.evidence: Slack ≤ 12: 6,061 cases (rule, reachable set, slack, last letter), 0 failures. Slack ≤ 14: ZERO fails in 1 of 904 situations, RUN(2, 1) in 2 of 1,344; PEAK holds in all 1,941. The missing patterns can still be completed, so they are not dead states. With multiplicity (number of placements per pattern) PEAK holds in all 2,812 tests at slack ≤ 6, ZERO and RUN(2, 1) fail. Recheck: python3 zero_fail.py 14 (12 minutes; prints the shortest failing words), run_rule.py 12 (50 seconds), count_rule.py 6 8.
nodes.refs: agents/interface/run_rule.py, zero_fail.py, count_rule.py, shorten.py (search that found the rules), letters_notes.md

nodes.title: Three shortening rules would settle 'within one mark'
nodes.intuition: The interface machine reads the word letter by letter and keeps the set of hole patterns that can be reached. If replacing a piece of the word by a longer piece never loses a reachable pattern, then the longer word is solvable whenever the shorter one is. Three such rules are enough for the family where every stone is within one mark of evenly spaced: (A) a zero may be doubled, (B) a zero may be replaced by + 0 −, (C) + − may be inserted anywhere. Any word of the family with a + in it contains + 0 … 0 −, possibly with no zeros. With no zeros, rule (C) backwards removes it. Otherwise rule (A) backwards shortens the zeros to one and rule (B) backwards turns + 0 − into 0. The word left at the end is all zeros, which is the anti-diagonal. For arrangements with distinct diagonals + − never occurs and rules (A), (B) suffice. No rule is true for a single hole pattern, only for the whole reachable set, and (A) is false for general words. Claim: the three rules hold after every prefix of the family.
nodes.statement: For a prefix x with letters in {−1, 0, +1} and partial sums ≥ 0 let F(x) be the set of interface states (pairs of diagrams) reachable after x. (A) F(x 0) ⊆ F(x 0 0). (B) F(x 0) ⊆ F(x + 0 −). (C) F(x) ⊆ F(x + −). All three hold for every such x.
nodes.example: P_n is + 0 … 0 −: rule (A) shortens it to + 0 −, rule (B) to 0.
nodes.evidence: All three hold for every prefix with slack ≤ 23 (233 distinct situations), so every word of the family with slack ≤ 23 is solvable for every n. No proof for all slacks: that needs a description of the reachable sets, or a direct way to turn a solution of the short word into one of the long word with the same hole pattern. Recheck: python3 l1_reduce.py 24 (1 minute).

nodes.title: Odd and even rows: a count every reachable hole pattern obeys
nodes.intuition: Colour the board like a chessboard. A stone with an even letter sits on a cell whose row and column have the same parity, a stone with an odd letter on a cell where they differ. Counting the four kinds of stones gives the number of each kind from the hole pattern alone: #(odd row, odd column) = (#odd(R) + #odd(C) − p)/2, and so on. All four must be between 0 and the number of letters of that parity. The number of odd rows in a hole pattern is what the 2-core of its diagram measures, so this is a condition on the two 2-cores. It explains the first missing patterns: the pair (staircase with t rows, staircase with t rows), which has slack t(t+1), cannot be reached before the prefix has t even letters. So the number of zeros needed before every pattern is reachable grows like the square root of the slack, and no bounded window can work. Claim: the two inequalities hold for every reachable state.
nodes.statement: Reflect the rows, so stone j has row + column = 2j + e_j. After a prefix of k stones with z even letters and p odd letters, every reachable state (R, C) (used rows, used columns) satisfies |#odd(R) − #odd(C)| ≤ p and |#odd(R) + #odd(C) − k| ≤ z.
nodes.example: After + + + + + + 0 the pattern ((2,1), (2,1)) is the only one of 65 missing: it would need two stones on (odd, odd) cells and there is one even letter.
nodes.evidence: Proof: count stones by (row parity, column parity); even letters give equal parities, odd letters unequal. The condition is far from exact: for words with letters −1, 0, +1 and distinct diagonals, slack ≤ 6 and length ≤ 9, of 1,935 unreachable (prefix, pattern) pairs it rules out 45; adding a sum test inside each parity class rules out 1,182. The rest need the same split repeated on rows mod 4, 8, …: e.g. after + + + + the pattern rows {1,2,3,6}, columns {1,2,4,5} fails because no free cell has row + column = 9.

nodes.title: Plus and minus stones next to the main diagonal
nodes.intuition: In the witnesses of P_n and of + + 0 − − the + and − stones sit right next to the main diagonal and only the 0 stones move far. If that were always possible, the + and − stones would be fixed up to a two-way choice and the problem would become: pair the remaining rows with the remaining columns so that the midpoints are exactly the positions of the zeros. Claim: such a witness always exists.
nodes.statement: Every word with letters −1, 0, +1 (distinct diagonals) has a witness in which each + stone k is at (k, k+1) or (k+1, k) and each − stone at (k−1, k) or (k, k−1), in reflected rows.
nodes.example: + + 0 0 − − (n = 6) has no such witness; its witnesses move a − stone two rows away.
nodes.evidence: Fails for 1 of 17 words at n = 6, 106 of 423 at n = 10, 770 of 2,283 at n = 12. With the choice fixed (+ at (k, k+1), − at (k−1, k)) it already fails for + 0 0 −.

nodes.title: Two more zeros never lose a hole pattern
nodes.intuition: After a few stones with letter 0 the machine reaches every hole pattern (card 'Bounded slack'). The simplest reason would be that zeros only ever add patterns. One zero can swap patterns around, so the claim is for two. Claim: adding two zeros to a prefix keeps every reachable pattern.
nodes.statement: For every legal prefix x (any letters) after which a letter 0 is allowed, F(x) ⊆ F(x 0 0).
nodes.example: Fails first at slack 8, after a prefix ending in +1: 131 patterns are reachable and one of them is lost.
nodes.evidence: True for slack ≤ 7. With slack ≤ 12 it fails in 15 of 1,236 situations (reachable set, slack, last letter), first at slack 8. Among rewrites of at most 2 letters, four lose nothing for slack ≤ 12: (−1) → (0, −1), (−2) → (−2, 0), (−1, −1) → (−2, 0), (−1, −2) → (−2, −1). Inside the family with letters −1, 0, +1 the rule does hold (card 'Two shortening rules').

nodes.title: A rule that sees three diagonals ahead
nodes.intuition: With no lookahead there is no rule (card 'Online rule'). The next hope is a rule that looks a few stones ahead. Claim: seeing the current diagonal and the next three is enough for every slack bound.
nodes.statement: For every slack bound B there is a rule that places the k-th stone knowing only the diagonals of stones 1 … k+3.
nodes.example: Seeing three ahead is enough for slack ≤ 8 and fails at slack 9.
nodes.evidence: Exact game search, knowing L letters (the current one and L − 1 ahead): L = 1, 2 win only for B ≤ 2, L = 3 only for B ≤ 4, L = 4 only for B ≤ 8 (loses at B = 9 and 10). L = 5 wins at B = 9, 11, 13; B = 14 was not run. The thresholds 2, 4, 8 are the same as for an invariant that remembers L − 1 past letters (card 'Invariant from the slack and the last few diagonals'), so the lookahead needed seems to grow with the slack bound; whether some larger fixed lookahead works for all B is not settled.

nodes.title: Repairing from both ends works from every solution
nodes.intuition: The zigzag chain repairs the board from the bottom stone only, and from some solutions it loops. But the board is equally wrong at the top stone, which is one mark too high, and the same repair can be run downwards from there. A failed round of either kind leaves a different solution of the middle word, so the two kinds of rounds can be mixed. The round graph makes this exact: the solutions of the middle word are joined by failed rounds, and a loop of the one-ended chain is a closed walk in that graph. Claim: with rounds from both ends allowed, a successful round is reachable from every solution of every middle word, not only from specially built ones.
nodes.statement: Let M be a word as in the card 'Every stone within one mark of evenly spaced', w ANY witness of M, with corner stones added. A bottom round is the zigzag chain from the bottom stone (rows first or columns first) until the mark is on the top stone (success) or back on the bottom stone; a top round is the same from the top stone downwards (the top stone is one too high: swap it with the previous row or column, and so on). A round that comes back leaves another witness of M. From every w, some sequence of rounds that come back, followed by one that succeeds, exists; so a witness of + M − is reached.
nodes.example: n = 10, M = + 0 − + + 0 − −: from the 4 witnesses where the bottom chain loops, a round from the top succeeds.
nodes.evidence: True for all 596,013 witnesses (distinct boards) of all middle words up to n = 15. Bottom rounds alone fail for 4, 20, 88, 392, 1,604, 6,940 witnesses at n = 10 … 15. From n = 12 some witnesses have no successful single round of either kind (10, 42, 210, 922 at n = 12 … 15), so a mixed sequence is needed. Moving the two marks in any order (not in whole rounds) also always reaches a witness (n ≤ 13). No rule for the order of the rounds and no proof. It is not known whether this is more than 'a successful round exists somewhere and the round graph is connected'.

nodes.title: A loop is cured by flipping one block
nodes.intuition: The solutions the induction builds come in pairs: the chain can start with a row move or a column move, and these are the two ends of one leapfrog path. So every block inside M carries a two-way choice, and in small cases a loop is caused by two blocks whose choices clash. Claim: switching one block always removes the loop.
nodes.statement: With M = B_1 … B_k and K as in the card 'Every block lets each kind of move through', call the two results of the chain from the same start (rows first, columns first) siblings. If the chain from a_1 ⊕ … ⊕ a_k (a_i ∈ K(B_i), plus corner stones) closes into a loop, then for some i it reaches the last stone after a_i is replaced by its sibling.
nodes.example: n = 15, M = (+ 0 −)(+ + 0 − −)(+ + 0 − −) with all three built rows-first. The second block sends the mark back. Switching the first or the second block gets the mark past the second block, but for one of the two ways the inside of the second block can be built the third block then sends it back; switching the third block changes nothing.
nodes.evidence: True for every loop up to n = 14. Fails at n = 15 (the example); 138 of 42,052 loops up to n = 16 are not cured by one switch. Switching both the first and the third block cures the example.

nodes.title: Solutions are the ends of leapfrog paths
nodes.intuition: Take a solution, remove the top stone, and pull the stone in the last row (or column) back by one: the result is a smaller board with all stones right except one that is one short. Such near-solutions can be changed in exactly two ways that keep 'one stone is one short': swap that stone's row with the next row, or its column with the next column; the shortage passes to the other stone. Each change undoes itself, so alternating them traces a path that never branches. A path can only stop when the short stone sits in the last row or column, and those positions are exactly the solutions. Claim: solutions are the ends of these paths, two per path.
nodes.statement: Let D be valid of size n+1 with distinct diagonals and largest diagonal n−1 (last letter −1), and let b_1, …, b_n be the targets r′ + c of its other stones. Let X be the set of permutation matrices on [n]² with one marked stone whose sums r′ + c, with the marked one raised by 1, are b_1, …, b_n. Let R swap the marked stone's row with the next row and leave the mark in its row; C the same for columns. Then R and C are involutions on X, undefined only when the mark is in the last row (R) or last column (C); the components of X are alternating paths and cycles; and the number of witnesses of D is twice the number of paths.
nodes.example: D = {−1, 0, 1}, n = 2, targets 3 and 4. X has three states: stones (1,1), (2,2) with (1,1) marked; stones (1,2), (2,1) with either one marked. R and C join the first to the other two, so X is one path, and D has two witnesses, 1 3 2 and 2 1 3.
nodes.evidence: Proof: R swaps rows r, r+1 where the marked stone is in row r; the marked stone gains 1 and is now exact, the other loses 1 and is now the marked one, in row r; applying R again swaps back. A witness of D has its top stone at (n, n+1) or (n+1, n), since its sum is 2n+1; the stone in row n+1 (or column n+1) moved back by one gives a state with the mark in the last row (column), and conversely. With distinct diagonals the mark is never at (n, n), so these states are exactly the vertices with one edge. Checked against direct counts for n+1 ≤ 8. X is the union over j of the witnesses of 'D without its top stone, stone j one diagonal lower', so X is non-empty whenever one of those smaller arrangements is solvable.

nodes.title: Leapfrog paths never close up
nodes.intuition: If near-solutions could never run in a closed loop, any near-solution would lead to a solution, and near-solutions exist by induction on the size. Claim: there are no cycles.
nodes.statement: For D as in the parent card, X has no cycle component.
nodes.example: n + 1 = 10, word + + 0 − + + 0 − − −: 8 paths and 2 cycles.
nodes.evidence: No cycle for n+1 ≤ 9 (2,031 paths at 9). At n+1 = 10: 8 cycles against 12,216 paths, in 4 words. Every word still has a path.
